pulls: These are people whose circumstances do not account for their composure. The question arises because the hope is visible.
paras: Look closely at what Peter expects unbelievers to ask about. Not your doctrine of the atonement. Not your view of origins. They ask about the hope that is in you.

That tells you the situation Peter has in mind. These are people whose circumstances do not account for their composure. They are losing property and status and sometimes their lives, and they are not despairing, and the neighbors want to know why. The question arises because the hope is visible.

Which is a searching thought. If nobody ever asks, it may be because the hope is not showing — or because your circumstances are comfortable enough that your composure requires no explanation. And Peter adds the manner as carefully as the content: with humility and fear. A defense given with contempt has already lost, whatever its logic. The tone is part of the argument.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE RIGHTEOUS FOR THE UNRIGHTEOUS
paras: And then Peter grounds the whole thing where he always grounds it. Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God.

Every word bears weight. Once — the sacrifice is finished and unrepeatable. The righteous for the unrighteous — the exchange at the heart of the gospel, the innocent standing in for the guilty. And the purpose clause, which is the sweetest phrase in the letter: that he might bring you to God. The point of the cross was not merely to spare you something. It was to bring you somewhere — into the presence of God, which is the one place a sinner could never have gone on his own.

Peter then moves through some of the most debated verses in the New Testament — the proclamation to the spirits in prison, the days of Noah, the eight souls brought through water, and baptism as the corresponding figure. The details have been argued for centuries and godly readers land in different places. But the direction is unmistakable, and it is triumph. Whatever happened in that proclamation, it was not a defeat. And Peter is careful to say what baptism does and does not do: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God, and its saving power is through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

He ends where a suffering church needs to end: who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him. The authorities you are afraid of are already subject to the One you belong to.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FROM DUST TO A HOPE WORTH DEFENDING
paras: Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been worn down until it has nothing gracious left to give: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV). And the reviving word this week is that you were called to bless — and that the strength for it comes from a settled heart, not a full tank.

So this week, do the inward work first. Sanctify Christ as Lord in your heart before the provocation arrives, because you will not do it in the moment. Then guard your mouth, especially with the people nearest you, because that is where the retaliation actually happens. And live a life composed enough that somebody eventually asks you why.

And when they ask, answer with humility and fear — not because your hope is uncertain, but because the One you are speaking about suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. Lift your eyes off the powers that frighten you and onto the Christ at the right hand, to whom they are already subject.

stations.verse: Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous.
stations.question: Has pressure made me harder toward the people closest to me — and have I told myself I earned the right?
stations.gloss: tenderhearted; moved in the inward parts
body: Eusplanchnos is built on splanchna, the inward organs — where the ancients located the deepest feelings, and the same root behind the verb used when Jesus was moved with compassion at the sight of a crowd. It is not politeness. It is being physically moved by another person’s condition. Peter puts it in a list of five aimed entirely at how believers treat believers, and he puts it there before he says anything about defending the faith to outsiders. He knows what pressure does to a church: squeezed from without, it begins eating itself within. The dust whispers that suffering has purchased you a little license to be sharp. Peter closes that door before he opens any other.
stations.live: Name the fellow believer you have been coolest toward this month. This week, move toward them once — not with a correction, with kindness.

stations.verse: Not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this.
stations.question: Am I settling for not retaliating — when Peter says the calling is to actively bless?
stations.gloss: to bless; to speak well of, to invoke good upon
body: Eulogeō is literally to speak well — and Peter does not merely forbid the return blow, he requires its opposite. There is no neutral middle where a Christian withholds retaliation and simply goes cold. Note the grounds: you were called to this. Blessing your enemies is not an advanced discipline for unusually saintly believers; it is the ordinary content of the Christian calling. And note the promise attached — that you may inherit a blessing. The two are bound together, not as payment but as pattern: those who have received blessing from God become people who hand it on, and the handing on is part of the inheriting.
stations.live: Take the person you would most like to answer sharply. This week, say one genuinely good thing about them to someone else — and mean it.

stations.verse: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.
stations.question: Is my readiness to explain my faith rooted in technique — or in a heart where Christ has already been enthroned?
stations.gloss: a defense; the reasoned answer given in court
body: Apologia was a legal term — the speech a defendant made in his own defense. But see what stands in front of it: sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. The readiness is second; the inward enthroning is first. Peter is quoting Isaiah 8, where the prophet was told not to fear what the people feared but to set the Lord of hosts apart as holy — and the logic is that a heart with Christ enthroned has no room left for the fear that would otherwise dictate its answers. Note also what people ask about: not your doctrine of origins, but the hope that is in you. The question arises because circumstances do not account for the composure. And the manner is part of the argument — with humility and fear. A defense given with contempt has already lost.
stations.live: Settle the throne before the pressure comes. Each morning this week, say it before the day starts: ‘Christ is Lord here.’ You will not manage it mid-conversation if you have not done it beforehand.

stations.verse: Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God.
stations.question: Do I think of the cross mainly as rescue from something — or as the way into somewhere I could never otherwise go?
stations.gloss: to bring near; to lead someone into the presence of a king
body: Prosagō means to lead someone to another — and in the ancient world it carried the sense of presenting a person at court, conducting them into the presence of a king they could not have approached alone. Peter uses it for the purpose of the cross, and every word around it bears weight. Once: finished, unrepeatable. The righteous for the unrighteous: the innocent standing in for the guilty. And then the purpose clause, which may be the sweetest phrase in the letter — that he might bring you to God. The point of Calvary was not merely to spare you something. It was to conduct you somewhere: into the presence of God, the one place a sinner could never have gone on his own.
stations.live: This week, when you pray, name what it cost to get you into the room: ‘I am here because the righteous suffered for the unrighteous.’ Then stay a while, since the access was paid for.

stations.verse: This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
stations.question: Is my conscience actually clear before God — or have I been managing guilt rather than bringing it to the cross?
stations.gloss: conscience; the inward knowing that accuses or excuses
body: Syneidēsis is a knowing-with — the faculty by which a person stands beside himself and passes judgment on what he sees. Peter is careful about what baptism does and does not do: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal of a good syneidēsis toward God, and its saving power comes through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The water saves the way a wedding ring marries — truly, as the sign of a reality it does not itself create. And that is the mercy here. A guilty conscience cannot be argued into silence or outrun by good works; Hebrews says only the blood of Christ cleanses it. Peter ends the section with the church’s comfort: Christ is at God’s right hand, and the powers you fear are already subject to Him.
stations.live: Bring one thing to God this week that your conscience keeps returning to. Do not manage it — confess it, and then rest in the resurrection that makes the appeal valid.

practices.title: MOVE TOWARD THE ONE YOU HAVE GONE COLD ON
practices.body: Pressure hardens a church from the inside first. Name the fellow believer you have been coolest toward this month, and move toward them once this week — not with a correction, with kindness. Peter puts this before he says a word about defending the faith to outsiders.

practices.title: BLESS, DO NOT MERELY WITHHOLD
practices.body: There is no neutral middle where you skip the return blow and go cold instead. Take the person you would most like to answer sharply, and this week say one genuinely good thing about them to somebody else — and mean it. You were called to this.

practices.title: SETTLE THE THRONE BEFORE THE PRESSURE
practices.body: You will not enthrone Christ mid-conversation if you have not done it beforehand. Each morning this week, before the day begins, say it plainly to the Father: ‘Christ is Lord here.’ Readiness to answer is downstream of a heart already settled.

practices.title: STAY IN THE ROOM THAT WAS PAID FOR
practices.body: The cross did not merely spare you something; it conducted you into the presence of God. When you pray this week, name the cost of your access — ‘I am here because the righteous suffered for the unrighteous’ — and then stay a while. Access that expensive should not be used briefly.

practices.title: STOP MANAGING THE CONSCIENCE
practices.body: Bring one thing to God this week that your conscience keeps circling back to. Do not manage it, minimize it, or work it off. Confess it, and then rest where Peter rests — in a resurrection that makes the appeal of a good conscience valid.

title: A Reason for the Hope
subtitle: from dust to a hope worth defending
keyVerse: Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.

passage.text: Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous,
not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.
For, “He who would love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit.
Let him turn away from evil and do good. Let him seek peace and pursue it.
For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”
Now who will harm you if you become imitators of that which is good?
But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing well than for doing evil.
Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God, being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit,
in whom he also went and preached to the spirits in prison,
who before were disobedient, when God waited patiently in the days of Noah, while the ship was being built. In it, few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water.
This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you—not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,
who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE HOPE THAT ANSWERS
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about winning arguments with outsiders. It is about settling the throne inside, guarding the mouth with those nearest you, and living composed enough that somebody eventually asks you why.
lifePulls: The authorities you are afraid of are already subject to the One you belong to.
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are Lord here before anything happens today. Keep my tongue from evil, most of all with the people nearest me. When I am insulted, teach me to bless instead. You suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring me to God. I stand in the room You paid for. Let the hope in me show, and give me a plain answer when someone asks. Amen.
prayerLines: Lord Jesus, You are Lord here before anything happens today.
Keep my tongue from evil, most of all with the people nearest me.
When I am insulted, teach me to bless instead.
You suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous,
to bring me to God. I stand in the room You paid for.
Let the hope in me show,
and give me a plain answer when someone asks.
Amen.
bottomLine: Peter tells a pressured church to bless rather than return the insult, because it was called to this. He sets the order plainly: sanctify Christ as Lord in your heart first, and readiness to answer for your hope follows. Christ suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God, and every power you fear is already subject to Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the grievance you have been carrying into the room with you. You have been squeezed, and you know what being squeezed does — it makes a person short with the people nearest to him, and then it supplies a reason: I have earned this. After what I have been through, a little sharpness is fair. Peter closes that door before he opens any other. Be like-minded. Be tenderhearted. Do not return the insult. Bless instead, because you were called to this.

And then hear the order of the great command, because you probably have it backwards. It is not first always be ready to give an answer. It is first sanctify the Lord God in your hearts — settle the throne, give Christ the room, decide who is Lord before the pressure arrives. You will not manage that mid-conversation. But a heart where Christ is enthroned has no space left for the fear that would otherwise write your answers for you.

Then notice what your neighbors actually ask about. Not your arguments. Your hope. The question comes because your circumstances do not account for your composure, and people cannot leave that alone. Which means the most persuasive thing about you is not what you know but what is visibly holding you when it should not be.

And what is holding you is this: Christ suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, not merely to spare you something but to bring you somewhere — into the presence of God, the one room a sinner could never enter alone. He suffered once. He went down into the dust of death. He rose, and He is now at the right hand of God, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to Him. Every power you are afraid of is already under the feet of the One who owns you. Lift your eyes off the pressure and onto the risen Christ — and rise.
closingVerse: Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.
carry: If someone watched your hardest week closely, would anything about your composure raise a question they would have to ask you — and if not, what has gone quiet in your hope?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Peter has been describing what Christ did with suffering. Now he issues an order, and it is a military one: arm yourselves also with the same mind. Take up a weapon. Put on the armor. And the armor he hands you is a way of thinking.

That word therefore at the head of the chapter is doing real work. It reaches back to the cross — to the righteous suffering for the unrighteous — and says: now think that way yourself. The mind of Christ was a mind that had already accepted that the path to glory ran through suffering, and had settled the question in advance.

Here is where the dust lies to you. It tells you that you can decide about suffering when suffering arrives — that there is no need to settle anything now, that you will find the strength when you need it. And so the blow lands on an unarmed soul, and the questions it asks are the ones you have never thought through, and you go down. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that was not ready: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV). Peter’s reviving word is that a mind can be armed before the battle, and that the armor is the settled conviction that Christ’s way is worth it.

sections.heading: Enough of That
pulls: The first response to a changed life is usually not persecution but bewilderment — and then, because bewilderment is uncomfortable, resentment.
paras: Peter’s next line has a certain bracing bluntness: we have spent enough of our past time doing the desire of the Gentiles. Enough. There is a whole theology of repentance in that word.

He is not saying the old life was insufficiently enjoyed. He is saying the account is closed. A believer who has been armed with the mind of Christ looks back at the years spent serving his own appetites and does not calculate how much more he might squeeze out of them; he says enough, and turns.

And Peter is realistic about the cost of turning. They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot. That is a remarkably contemporary observation. The first response to a changed life is usually not persecution but bewilderment — and then, because bewilderment is uncomfortable, resentment. Peter tells his readers to expect it and not to be shaken by it. The people who cannot understand your restraint will one day give account to the same Judge who holds them and you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE END OF ALL THINGS IS NEAR
paras: Then Peter says something that ought to produce urgency, and watch what he actually does with it. But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.

If you had asked most people to complete that sentence, they would have reached for something dramatic — sell everything, flee to the hills, scan the headlines for signs. Peter reaches for sober-mindedness and prayer.

This is characteristic of the New Testament and worth learning. The nearness of the end does not produce frenzy in a Christian; it produces clarity. A soldier who knows the campaign is nearly over does not become careless or hysterical. He becomes focused. And notice where the focus lands: sober in prayer. The last-days believer is not chiefly a man with a chart. He is a man on his knees with a clear head.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: LOVE THAT COVERS
pulls: Love does not publish. It does not collect offenses, catalogue them, and produce the file at the useful moment.
paras: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins. Above all things — Peter ranks it first, ahead of everything else he is about to say.

The word for earnest is the stretching word from chapter one, the muscle extended to its limit. And what does that stretched love do? It covers. Peter is quoting Proverbs, and the picture is a garment thrown over something exposed. Be careful what this does and does not mean. It does not mean concealing sin from those who need to address it, and it never means covering for what harms the vulnerable. It means that love does not publish. It does not collect offenses, catalogue them, and produce the file at the useful moment. In a church under pressure, where everyone has failed everyone else in small ways, someone has to be willing to let things be covered rather than kept — and Peter says that is what love does. And then, with plain practicality, he adds: be hospitable to one another without grumbling. Open your home. And do not complain about it afterward.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: MANAGERS OF A GRACE THAT IS NOT YOURS
paras: Then Peter turns to gifts, and his framing is unusual. As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

Three things follow immediately. First, each has received — there are no giftless Christians in the New Testament, and the person convinced he has nothing to contribute is contradicting the apostle. Second, the gift is for serving one another, not for personal fulfillment. Third, and most searching, you are a manager. The word is the one used for the household steward who ran another man’s estate. He had real authority and no ownership. Everything he administered belonged to someone else.

And Peter’s two examples close every door to self-display. If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God — not your opinions dressed up. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies — not your own reserves, spent for your own credit. Both examples end at the same place: that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.

This is the difference between working from natural ability and working in the Spirit’s strength. When you function in natural ability, you quietly expect to be noticed. When you function in supplied strength, the arithmetic changes — because you cannot take credit for a strength you did not generate.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FROM DUST TO A LIFE POURED OUT
paras: Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has run out: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV). And the reviving word this week is that you were never meant to serve out of your own reserves. The strength is supplied. Your part is stewardship, not manufacture.

So arm yourself now, before you need the armor. Settle in advance that the path to glory runs through suffering, because Christ’s did. Say enough to the years already spent. Let the nearness of the end make you clear-headed rather than frantic. Stretch your love until it covers rather than collects. Open your home and do not grumble about it.

And when you serve, remember whose estate this is. You are a steward of grace in its various forms — a manager of something that was never yours — so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. Lift your eyes off your own dwindling reserves and onto the strength that God supplies.

stations.verse: Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind.
stations.question: Have I settled in advance that the path to glory may run through suffering — or am I planning to decide when it arrives?
stations.gloss: to arm; to equip a soldier with weapons
body: Hoplizō appears only here in the New Testament, and it is a soldier’s word — from hoplon, a weapon or piece of armor. Peter issues it as an order, and the armor he hands you is a way of thinking: the same mind Christ had, which had already accepted that the road to glory ran through suffering and had settled the question in advance. That is what armor is for. Nobody puts it on during the battle. The dust tells you there is no need to decide anything now, that strength will arrive when it is needed — and then the blow lands on an unarmed soul, asking questions you have never thought through.
stations.live: Settle one question this week before you need the answer: ‘If this costs me, is Christ still worth it?’ Say yes now, in the quiet, while nothing is on fire.

stations.verse: But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self- controlled, and sober in prayer.
stations.question: Does the nearness of the end make me frantic and distracted — or clear-headed and praying?
stations.gloss: to be sober; clear-headed, unintoxicated in judgment
body: Nēphō literally means to be free from the influence of wine, and the New Testament uses it almost entirely in a figurative sense: a mind not clouded, not swayed, seeing things as they actually are. Notice what Peter does with the nearness of the end. If asked to complete that sentence, most men would reach for something dramatic. Peter reaches for sober-mindedness and prayer. That is characteristic of the whole New Testament: eschatology produces clarity, not frenzy. The man who knows the end is near does not panic; he steadies. The last-days Christian is not chiefly a man with a chart. He is a man on his knees with a clear head.
stations.live: Name what has been intoxicating your judgment lately — a news cycle, a worry, a screen. Cut its intake this week and put the reclaimed time into sober prayer.

stations.verse: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
stations.question: Is my home genuinely open — and if it is, do I quietly resent the cost afterward?
stations.gloss: hospitable; literally a lover of strangers
body: Philoxenos is built from phileō, to love, and xenos, a stranger — and it is the exact opposite of the word English has made from the same root, xenophobia. In the first century this was not entertaining; it was survival infrastructure. Traveling believers and displaced Christians depended on open homes, and inns were dangerous and disreputable. Peter’s addition is the honest part: without grumbling. He knows that hospitality is costly in a way guests rarely see, and that the sin most native to it is not refusal but resentment afterward. A home opened and then complained about has given with one hand and taken back with the other.
stations.live: Open your home once this week to someone who cannot reciprocate. Then watch the conversation afterward, and refuse to tally the cost out loud.

stations.verse: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.
stations.question: Am I holding what God gave me as property to enjoy — or as an estate I am managing for its Owner?
stations.gloss: a steward; the manager of another man’s household
body: Oikonomos was the household steward who ran an estate on behalf of its owner — often a trusted slave with real authority over considerable wealth, and no ownership of any of it. Peter chooses it deliberately. Three things follow at once. Each has received: there are no giftless Christians in the New Testament, and the believer convinced he has nothing to contribute is contradicting an apostle. The gift is for serving one another, not for personal fulfillment. And you are a manager, which means the question at the end is not how much you enjoyed the estate but whether you were found faithful with it.
stations.live: Name one thing God has given you that you have been holding as private property. This week, spend it once on someone else, as a steward rather than an owner.

stations.verse: If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
stations.question: Am I serving out of my own dwindling reserves — and then quietly expecting to be noticed for it?
stations.gloss: to supply lavishly; to bear the whole cost of a production
body: Chorēgeō has a marvelous history. In classical Athens the chōrēgos was the wealthy citizen who personally underwrote an entire dramatic chorus — costumes, training, musicians, the whole production — at his own expense. The word came to mean supplying abundantly, bearing the full cost. Peter says: serve out of the strength God chorēgeōs. Not your reserves. His provision, lavishly furnished. And notice how that changes the arithmetic of credit. Work out of your own reserves and credit starts to feel owed; work out of what God supplies and taking credit becomes incoherent — which is exactly why Peter ends the verse where he does: that in all things God may be glorified.
stations.live: Before the task that most depletes you this week, stop and ask for supply rather than gritting your teeth: ‘I am out. Furnish this.’ Then let the credit go where it belongs.

practices.title: SETTLE IT IN THE QUIET
practices.body: Armor is never put on during the battle. This week, while nothing is on fire, settle one question with the Father in advance: ‘If following You costs me this, is Christ still worth it?’ Say yes now. An unarmed mind gets asked questions mid-blow that it has never thought through.

practices.title: SAY ENOUGH AND MEAN IT
practices.body: Peter’s word for the old life is bracing: we have spent enough of our past time. Name one appetite you have been quietly calculating how much more you can get from, and close the account this week. Repentance is not negotiation; it is a turn.

practices.title: TRADE FRENZY FOR CLARITY
practices.body: Name what has been clouding your judgment — a news cycle, a worry loop, a screen. Cut its intake this week and put the reclaimed time into prayer. The nearness of the end is meant to make you sober and focused, not frantic and scattered.

practices.title: COVER RATHER THAN COLLECT
practices.body: Ask the Spirit whether you have been quietly keeping a file on someone. This week, let one offense be covered rather than kept — not concealed from those who must address it, but simply not published, not catalogued, not produced at the useful moment. Love does not publish.

practices.title: ASK FOR SUPPLY BEFORE THE TASK
practices.body: Before the thing that most depletes you this week, stop and ask rather than grit: ‘I am out. Furnish this.’ You are a steward of another man’s estate, working from strength He supplies — which means the credit was never going to be yours anyway.

title: Armed with the Mind of Christ
subtitle: from dust to a life poured out
keyVerse: Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.

passage.text: Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin,
that you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God.
For we have spent enough of our past time doing the desire of the Gentiles, and having walked in lewdness, lusts, drunken binges, orgies, carousings, and abominable idolatries.
They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming.
They will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.
For to this end the Good News was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed as men in the flesh, but live as to God in the spirit.
But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE ARMED MIND
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about summoning more strength. It is about arming your mind before the blow lands, and then serving out of a supply that is furnished rather than manufactured.
lifePulls: You cannot take credit for a strength you did not generate — which is precisely why Peter ends where he does: that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
prayer: Father, settle it in me now, before the blow: Christ is worth it. I have spent enough of my past time on the old life. Make me sober-minded and clear, not frantic. Stretch my love until it covers instead of keeping score. Open my home and my hands without grumbling. I serve today out of the strength You supply, not my own. In all things, be glorified through Jesus Christ. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, settle it in me now, before the blow: Christ is worth it.
I have spent enough of my past time on the old life.
Make me sober-minded and clear, not frantic.
Stretch my love until it covers instead of keeping score.
Open my home and my hands without grumbling.
I serve today out of the strength You supply, not my own.
In all things, be glorified through Jesus Christ.
Amen.
bottomLine: Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourself with the same mind, and close the account on the old life. The nearness of the end produces sober prayer, love that covers rather than collects, and hospitality without grumbling. The dust says you will find strength when you need it; Peter says serve now, as a steward, out of the strength God supplies.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off your own dwindling reserves. You have been trying to be strong out of a tank you already know is empty, and the dust has been telling you that this is what faithfulness feels like. It is not. Peter’s word for the strength a Christian serves from is the word for a wealthy patron who underwrote an entire production out of his own pocket — costumes, chorus, musicians, all of it. God does not ask you to fund the performance. He asks you to steward what He furnishes.

But first, arm yourself. Peter gives an order, and the armor he hands you is a way of thinking — the same mind Christ had, which had already decided, long before Gethsemane, that the road to glory ran through suffering. Nobody puts armor on during the battle. So settle it now, in the quiet, while nothing is on fire: if this costs me, He is worth it.

And then close the account. We have spent enough of our past time. Enough. Not a calculation about how much more the old appetites might yield, but a turn — and yes, the people around you will find it strange, and strangeness curdles into resentment, and Peter tells you to expect that and not be shaken by it. They will answer to the same Judge who holds you, and He is not confused about any of it.

So let the nearness of the end make you clear rather than frantic. Let your love stretch until it covers instead of collecting. Let your door open, and do not tally the cost out loud. And when you serve, remember whose estate this is — that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever. Lift your eyes off your empty tank and onto the God who supplies — and rise.
closingVerse: If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever.
carry: What question about the cost of following Christ have you been leaving unsettled — and what would it mean to answer it this week, in the quiet, before you need the armor?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Beloved, don’t be astonished. Peter opens with a term of deep affection and then immediately corrects an expectation, and the combination tells you what kind of pastor he is. He is not scolding. He is removing a weight his readers should never have been carrying.

The weight is surprise. Peter says the fiery trial has come to test you — that it has a purpose — and that it is not a strange thing. And that second point may be the more urgent of the two, because a great deal of Christian suffering is doubled by astonishment. The pain itself is one burden. The bewilderment that this is happening at all — the sense that God has broken the arrangement, that something has gone off the rails — is a second burden, and it is often heavier than the first.

Here is where the dust lies to you. It tells you that trouble in a believer’s life is evidence of a malfunction. That if God were pleased with you, the road would be smoother. That your suffering is either His punishment or His absence. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul flattened by that interpretation: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV). Peter’s reviving word removes the surprise entirely and puts something else in its place — participation.

sections.heading: You Are Sharing His Sufferings
pulls: A great deal of Christian suffering is doubled by astonishment. The pain is one burden. The bewilderment that this is happening at all is a second, and it is often heavier.
paras: But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.

This is a staggering claim, and it deserves care. Peter is not saying your suffering atones for anything; he has already been at pains to say that Christ suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous. He is saying that when you suffer for Christ’s sake, you are not suffering at a distance from Him. You are in it with Him. There is a fellowship in it.

That is why the command is rejoice and not merely endure. Peter is not asking anyone to pretend the fire is pleasant. He is pointing at what the fire means: that you belong to Him closely enough to share what came to Him. And he attaches it to a horizon — at the revelation of his glory. Glory follows suffering. It did for Christ, and Peter, who saw both the transfiguration and the crucifixion, is not speculating.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE SPIRIT RESTS ON YOU
paras: Then Peter says something almost too good to receive at face value: if you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

The verb is the language of the shekinah — the glory that settled on the tabernacle and filled the temple, that came down and stayed. Peter says that in the moment you are being insulted for Christ’s name, that glory is resting on you.

Take the ordinary shape of it. The remark at work. The eye-roll. The relative who has decided your faith is an embarrassment. In that moment, the dust says you have been diminished — made smaller, exposed, foolish. Peter says the exact opposite is happening where you cannot see. The Spirit of glory is settling on you like the cloud on the tent. What feels like the moment of your humiliation is the moment of your greatest visible dignity, if you had eyes for the invisible.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: BUT MAKE SURE IT IS THE RIGHT FIRE
pulls: Ask the honest question: is this the cost of Christ, or the cost of me? Peter puts the interfering busybody in the same sentence as the thief.
paras: Peter is too honest a pastor to leave that unqualified, so he adds a bracing caution. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer, or a meddler in other men’s matters.

The list starts severe and ends almost comically ordinary. Murderer, thief, evildoer — and then meddler, a busybody in other people’s affairs. Peter puts the interfering church member in the same sentence as the criminal, and the point is that a great deal of the trouble a Christian takes for persecution is nothing of the kind. Some of it is simply the consequence of his own sin, and some of it is the entirely predictable result of being tiresome.

This matters pastorally in both directions. It protects a suffering saint from false comfort, and it protects him from false guilt. Ask the honest question: is this the cost of Christ, or the cost of me? And then, having asked it, Peter says: if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this matter. Shame is the enemy’s instrument here. Peter knew that firsthand — he had once warmed his hands at a fire and denied he knew the man.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: JUDGMENT BEGINS AT THE HOUSE OF GOD
paras: Then Peter reframes the whole thing in a way that is startling and, once you see it, deeply reassuring. For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God. If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?

He is looking at the fire and calling it judgment — God’s judgment, moving through the earth, and beginning at His own house. But mark the difference in what it does. When the fire reaches the church, it is purifying; it burns away what does not belong and leaves what is real. When it reaches those outside, there is nothing to refine.

This is why the same fire is not the same event for a believer and an unbeliever. It is the difference between a refiner’s crucible and a consuming blaze. The dust looks at the flames around a Christian and says God is against you. Peter says: God is at work in His house, and He always starts with what He loves most, because He intends to keep it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FROM DUST THROUGH THE FIRE
paras: And then the last verse, which gathers everything: let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.

Every phrase is load-bearing. According to the will of God — the suffering is not outside His government. In doing good — keep doing right in the middle of it; do not let the fire make you bitter or idle. Entrust their souls — the verb is a banking word, to deposit something valuable with a trusted keeper. And then the title Peter chooses for God, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament: a faithful Creator.

Not a faithful Judge. Not a faithful Redeemer, though He is both. Creator — because a soul in the fire needs to know that the One holding it is the same One who made it out of the dust of the ground in the first place. He knows the material. He knows exactly what it can bear. And He has never yet mishandled what He made.

So this week, do the depositing. Take the soul you are anxious about — your own — and put it in the keeping of the faithful Creator. Keep doing good while you wait. And do not be astonished by the fire. Lift your eyes off the flames and onto the God who is refining, not consuming.

stations.verse: Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you.
stations.question: How much of my present pain is the trouble itself — and how much is astonishment that it is happening to me at all?
stations.gloss: a burning; the smelting fire of a refiner
body: Pyrōsis is not the word for a house burning down. It belongs to the smelting furnace — the deliberate, controlled heat a refiner applies to ore, at a temperature he chooses, for exactly as long as it takes. Malachi pictures God sitting as a refiner of silver, watching. Peter calls the trial a pyrōsis and says it has come to test you, which means it has a purpose and a purposer. And he tells them not to be astonished, because astonishment is a second burden laid on top of the first. The pain is one weight. The bewilderment that God has broken the arrangement is another, and it is often heavier. Peter removes it in a sentence.
stations.live: Separate the two weights this week. Name the trial, and then name the astonishment underneath it — and let Peter’s word take the second one off you.

stations.verse: But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.
stations.question: Do I experience my suffering as isolation from Christ — or as something I am in together with Him?
stations.gloss: to share in; to have fellowship, to hold in common
body: Koinōneō is the fellowship word — to have something in common, to be a partner in it. Peter is not saying your suffering atones; he has already insisted Christ suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous. He is saying that when you suffer for Christ’s sake you do not suffer at a distance from Him. There is partnership in it. That is why the command is rejoice and not merely endure: not because the fire is pleasant, but because of what it means that you are in it with Him. And Peter attaches a horizon — at the revelation of His glory. Glory follows suffering. It did for Christ, and Peter saw both the transfiguration and the cross.
stations.live: The next time the cost lands this week, say it plainly: ‘This is not distance from You. This is fellowship with You.’ Then look up at the horizon Peter names.

stations.verse: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.
stations.question: When I am made to feel small for Christ’s sake, do I read that moment as diminishment — or as glory settling?
stations.gloss: to rest upon; to settle down and remain
body: Anapauō means to come to rest and stay — the language used of the Spirit resting on the promised Branch in Isaiah, and behind it the shekinah cloud that settled on the tabernacle and filled the temple. Peter says that in the moment you are insulted for Christ’s name, that glory is resting on you. Take the ordinary shape of it: the remark at work, the eye-roll, the relative who finds your faith embarrassing. The dust says you have been made smaller and more foolish. Peter says the opposite is happening where you cannot see. What feels like the moment of your humiliation is the moment of your greatest dignity, if you had eyes for the invisible.
stations.live: Recall the last time you were quietly embarrassed for Christ. Reinterpret it this week: ‘The Spirit of glory was resting on me in that room, and I did not see it.’

stations.verse: Let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him.
stations.question: What am I still holding that I have never actually deposited with God?
stations.gloss: to entrust; to deposit for safekeeping
body: Paratithēmi is a banking word. In a world without secure institutions, a man leaving on a journey would deposit his valuables with a trusted friend, and the arrangement was held sacred. Peter says: do that with your soul. And notice the two conditions around the deposit. According to the will of God — the suffering is not outside His government. In doing good — keep doing right in the middle of it; do not let the fire make you bitter or idle. This is the same word Jesus used from the cross when He said, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. Peter is teaching his readers to die the way his Lord died, and to live that way first.
stations.live: Take the thing you are most anxious about this week and make an actual deposit of it: ‘Into Your hands. This is Yours to keep.’ Then leave it in the vault.

stations.verse: …as to a faithful Creator.
stations.question: Do I trust that the One holding me in the fire knows exactly what I am made of and what I can bear?
stations.gloss: Creator; the one who founds and makes
body: Ktistēs appears exactly once in the New Testament — here, at the end of a chapter about fire. Peter had every title available to him. He could have written faithful Judge, or faithful Redeemer, and both are true. He chose Creator, and the choice is pastoral genius. A soul in the furnace needs to know that the One holding it is the same One who formed it from the dust of the ground and breathed into it. He knows the material. He knows how you are made. He remembers that you are dust. He knows precisely what this vessel can bear, because He made it — and He has never once mishandled what He made.
stations.live: When the trial feels beyond your capacity this week, take it to the One who built the capacity: ‘You made me. You know what I can bear. I am not telling You something You do not know.’

practices.title: PUT DOWN THE ASTONISHMENT
practices.body: Separate the two weights you are carrying. Name the trial itself, and then name the surprise underneath it — the sense that God has broken the arrangement. Peter removes the second one in a sentence: this is not a strange thing. Let him take it off you this week.

practices.title: NAME IT FELLOWSHIP
practices.body: The next time the cost lands, say it plainly to the Son: ‘This is not distance from You. This is fellowship with You.’ You are not suffering at a distance from Christ but sharing in what came to Him — and glory follows suffering, as it did for Him.

practices.title: ASK THE HONEST QUESTION
practices.body: Peter puts the meddler beside the thief for a reason. Ask the Father honestly this week whether your present trouble is the cost of Christ or the cost of you. The question protects you from false comfort in one direction and false guilt in the other — and you need both protections.

practices.title: REFUSE THE SHAME
practices.body: If you are suffering as a Christian, Peter says do not be ashamed but glorify God in that name. Peter knew shame firsthand; he had warmed his hands at a fire and denied he knew the man. This week, name one place you have been quietly embarrassed for Christ, and stop being.

practices.title: MAKE AN ACTUAL DEPOSIT
practices.body: Take the thing you are most anxious about and deposit it with the Spirit’s help, using your Lord’s own words: ‘Into Your hands. This is Yours to keep.’ Then leave it in the vault. A deposit you keep withdrawing was never really made.

title: The Fiery Trial
subtitle: from dust through the fire
keyVerse: Let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.

passage.text: Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you.
But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.
For let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer, or a meddler in other men’s matters.
But if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter.
For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God. If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?
“If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?”
Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE REFINING FIRE
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about escaping the fire. It is about laying down the astonishment, doing good in the middle of it, and depositing your soul with the One who made it.
lifePulls: He could have written faithful Judge, or faithful Redeemer. He chose faithful Creator — because a soul in the furnace needs to know that the One holding it is the One who formed it from the dust.
prayer: Faithful Creator, You made me, and You know what I can bear. I put down my astonishment at this fire. It is not a strange thing. It is a share in Christ’s sufferings. If it is the cost of my own sin, show me, and I will turn. If it is the cost of His name, keep me from shame. Into Your hands I entrust my soul today. Keep me doing good in the middle of it. Amen.

I put down my astonishment at this fire.
It is not a strange thing. It is a share in Christ’s sufferings.

bottomLine: Do not be astonished at the fiery trial: it is a refiner’s furnace, and sharing Christ’s sufferings is fellowship with Christ. Make sure it is the right fire and not the cost of your own sin. Then keep doing good and entrust your soul to a faithful Creator — the One who formed you from the dust and knows exactly what the vessel can bear.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the flames. And before anything else, put down the weight you were never meant to carry — the astonishment. You have been hurting, and underneath the hurting has been a second and heavier thing: the sense that something has gone wrong, that God has broken the arrangement, that this was not supposed to happen to someone who was trying. Beloved, Peter says, don’t be astonished. He calls you beloved in the same breath. That is not a scolding. That is a pastor lifting a burden off your back.

Because the fire is not a house burning down. The word Peter uses belongs to the smelting furnace — deliberate heat, at a temperature the refiner chooses, for exactly as long as it takes. Malachi saw Him sitting there, watching the silver. He is not absent from your furnace. He is seated beside it, and He is not distracted, and He will not leave it too long.

And here is what is actually happening in the moment you feel smallest. When you are insulted for the name of Christ — the remark, the eye-roll, the relative who finds your faith an embarrassment — the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. That is the word for the cloud that settled on the tabernacle and filled the temple. What feels like your humiliation is your greatest visible dignity, if you had eyes for the invisible.

So keep doing good in the middle of it. Do not let the fire make you bitter or idle. And then do the one thing Peter tells a burning church to do: make the deposit. Take the soul you are so anxious about and hand it over for safekeeping — the same word your Lord used when He said Father, into your hands. And notice who receives it: not a faithful Judge, not a faithful Redeemer, though He is both. A faithful Creator. The One who formed you out of the dust of the ground knows exactly what this vessel can bear, because He made it. Lift your eyes off the flames and onto the hands that made you — and rise.
closingVerse: Let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.
carry: What have you been carrying as astonishment rather than as trial — and what would change this week if you simply stopped being surprised that following Christ costs something?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Peter has spent five chapters on suffering, and now he closes. And a man’s closing words tell you what he most wants remembered. Peter’s are about the church — its shepherds, its young, its unity, its enemy, and the God who will finish what He began.

He introduces himself with unusual tenderness: a fellow elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and who will also share in the glory that will be revealed. Not an apostle, though he was. Fellow elder. He is standing beside them, not above them — which is the whole burden of the chapter he is about to write.

Here is where the dust lies to you, and this may be its subtlest lie of all. It tells you that the way up is up. That the answer to being low is to elevate yourself: to be seen, to be right, to be needed, to secure your position. And so the anxious soul spends itself climbing, and the climbing produces the very exhaustion it was meant to cure. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has climbed and fallen: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV). And Peter’s reviving word is the most counterintuitive sentence in the letter: humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The way up is down, and the lifting is His work, not yours.

sections.heading: Shepherds Who Do Not Lord It
pulls: The dust tells you the way up is up. Peter says the way up is down, and the lifting is His work, not yours.
paras: Peter’s charge to elders is a charge about motive as much as duty. Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock. Three contrasts, and each names a way pastoral work goes wrong. Compulsion — doing it because you are trapped rather than because you love it. Dishonest gain — using the flock rather than feeding it. Lording it over — leading by weight of position rather than by weight of example.

And notice the possessive that governs everything: the flock of God. Not the elder’s flock. He is a steward, not an owner, and the sheep were bought with blood that was not his. Then Peter names the reward, and it is not a salary or a reputation: when the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away. That word for the crown is a flower word — a wreath woven of the amaranth, the bloom the ancients prized because it kept its color even when dried. Every earthly wreath browns. This one does not.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: TIE ON THE APRON
paras: Then Peter gives an image so vivid it is a wonder the church has made it sound so bland. All of you clothe yourselves with humility.

The verb is a rare one, and it does not mean simply to put on a garment. It means to tie on the apron a slave wore over his clothing for menial work — knotted at the front, the visible badge of someone who serves.

Peter is remembering something. There was a night when his Master rose from supper, laid aside His outer garment, tied a towel around Himself, and knelt down to wash the feet of men who would shortly abandon Him. Peter had objected. He had said You will never wash my feet!, because he could not bear to see the world’s order inverted in front of him.
Thirty years later, an old man writes to churches he will never see again and reaches for that exact image. Tie on the apron. He is not giving them an abstraction. He is giving them a memory.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: CAST IT, BECAUSE HE CARES
pulls: Pride and worry share a root: both assume the outcome depends on you. Pride says I can secure this; worry says I must secure this and I cannot.
paras: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

Notice that humility and anxiety are treated as one subject. That connection is easy to miss and worth pausing over, because at first they seem unrelated. But pride and worry share a root: both assume that the outcome depends on you. Pride says I can secure this; worry says I must secure this and I cannot. They are the same conviction in different moods.

So Peter deals with them together. Get low under God’s mighty hand — and while you are down there, throw everything you are carrying onto Him. The verb is forceful, the same word used for the garments flung over the colt on Palm Sunday. Not set down gently. Thrown.

And then the reason, which is the tenderest clause in the letter: because he cares for you. Not because worry is unproductive. Not because you ought to be stronger. Because it matters to Him. The God whose hand is mighty enough to be worth submitting to is the God to whom you personally matter.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: A LION, AND A BROTHERHOOD
paras: Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Withstand him steadfast in your faith.

Peter names the enemy plainly, and he had reason to. Jesus once told him that Satan had demanded to sift him like wheat — and then added, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. Peter went down that night. He also got up, because Someone was praying for him.

Two things about the resistance Peter prescribes. First, it is steadfast in your faith — standing, not attacking. You resist a lion by refusing to run. Second, he adds a strange comfort: knowing that your brothers who are in the world are undergoing the same sufferings. Not you are the only one. You are one of a great company presently under the same pressure. Isolation is the lion’s favorite ground, and Peter takes it away from him in a sentence.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FROM DUST TO ETERNAL GLORY
paras: And then the letter opens out into one of the great sentences of the New Testament. May the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.

Look at what is packed in. He is the God of all grace — every kind you will need. He has called you to his eternal glory, and the calling is effectual. The suffering is a little while, measured against eternity. And then four verbs, and the two words standing in front of them: he himself will do it. Mend what is broken. Set it on a foundation. Give it strength. Settle it so it does not shift.

That is the answer to every fear a suffering Christian carries about whether he will make it. You will not restore yourself. He will. And Peter, who denied his Lord beside a fire and was restored beside another one on a beach, is the right man to tell you so.

So the letter that opened with a living hope closes with a settled one. This is the true grace of God in which you stand. Stand in it. Clothe yourself with humility. Throw your anxieties on the God to whom you matter. Resist the lion by refusing to run. And lift your eyes off the little while and onto the eternal glory to which you have been called — from dust, to living hope, to glory.

stations.verse: When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away.
stations.question: Whose approval am I actually working for — and would I still serve if the only recognition came at His appearing?
stations.gloss: Chief Shepherd; the one over all the under-shepherds
body: Archipoimēn occurs only here in the New Testament. He has just told the elders to shepherd the flock of God — not theirs — and now he names the Owner. Every pastor is an under-shepherd; the sheep were bought with blood that was not his. And the reward Peter names is not a salary or a reputation but an unfading crown. The word for it is a flower word: the amaranth was prized in the ancient world because it kept its color even when dried. Every earthly wreath browns within days. This one does not, and it is handed out by the Chief Shepherd Himself.
stations.live: Name the recognition you have been quietly working for this year. Hand it over this week: ‘If the only crown comes at Your appearing, that is enough.’

stations.verse: All of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’
stations.question: Where am I holding position when I could be tying on the apron?
stations.gloss: to tie on; to fasten a servant’s apron over one’s clothing
body: Enkomboomai appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it is far more specific than put on. The enkombōma was the apron a slave knotted over his clothing for menial work — the visible badge of someone who serves. Peter is remembering something. There was a night when his Master rose from supper, laid aside His outer garment, tied a towel around Himself, and knelt to wash the feet of men who would shortly abandon Him — and Peter objected, because he could not bear to watch the world’s order inverted in front of him. Thirty years later the old man reaches for that exact image. He is not handing his readers an abstraction. He is handing them a memory.
stations.live: Do one genuinely menial thing for someone this week that nobody will see or credit. Tie the apron on deliberately, and notice what it does to your heart.

stations.verse: Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
stations.question: What am I still carrying that I have been setting down gently and picking straight back up?
stations.gloss: to cast upon; to fling something onto another
body: Epirrhiptō is a forceful verb — the same word Luke uses for the garments thrown over the colt on Palm Sunday. Not set down gently. Flung. And notice what Peter attaches it to: it hangs on the humbling of the previous verse, because pride and worry share a root. Both assume the outcome depends on you; pride says I can secure this and worry says I must secure this and I cannot. So Peter deals with them together. Get low under the mighty hand, and while you are down there, throw everything you are carrying onto Him. Then comes the tenderest clause in the letter — because he cares for you. Not because anxiety is unproductive. Because it matters to Him.
stations.live: Name the worry you keep setting down politely and retrieving. This week, throw it: ‘This is Yours. You care about me, and I am not carrying it back out of this room.’

stations.verse: Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.
stations.question: Am I taking the enemy seriously without being afraid of him — and have I let isolation become his ground?
stations.gloss: an adversary; the opposing party in a lawsuit
body: Antidikos is a courtroom word — the opponent in a legal case, the one pressing charges. Zechariah saw exactly this: Satan standing at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the Lord rebuking the accuser and clothing the filthy priest in clean garments. Peter had personal reason to name him. Jesus once told him Satan had demanded to sift him like wheat, and then added, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. Peter went down that night. He also got up, because Someone was praying for him. And note the resistance prescribed: steadfast in your faith — standing, not attacking. You resist a lion by refusing to run.
stations.live: Refuse isolation this week, since it is the lion’s favorite ground. Tell one trusted believer the thing you have been carrying alone.

stations.verse: May the God of all grace… after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.
stations.question: Do I believe my restoration is finally my project — or His?
stations.gloss: to mend; to repair a net, to make complete
body: Katartizō is a restoring word with wonderfully concrete uses. Mark uses it of fishermen mending their nets; physicians used it for setting a broken bone. It means taking something torn or out of joint and putting it back into working order. Peter places it first among four verbs — mend, establish, strengthen, settle — and in front of them stands the decisive phrase: he himself will do it. Not you. And Peter, who unravelled beside one fire and was mended beside another on a beach, is exactly the right man to promise it. The suffering is a little while; the glory you were called to is eternal. He does not merely get you through. He repairs the tear.
stations.live: Name the place you are most torn right now. Bring it to Him this week as a net to be mended, not a failure to be hidden: ‘You said You would do this Yourself.’

practices.title: HAND OVER THE RECOGNITION
practices.body: Name the recognition you have been quietly working for this year — the notice, the thanks, the position. Hand it to the Father this week: ‘If the only crown comes at Your appearing, that is enough.’ Every earthly wreath browns; the unfading one is given by the Chief Shepherd Himself.

practices.title: TIE ON THE APRON
practices.body: Do one genuinely menial thing for someone this week that nobody will see or credit. Tie it on deliberately, remembering the night your Master knelt with a towel before men who were about to abandon Him. Then notice what the doing of it does to your heart.

practices.title: THROW IT, DO NOT SET IT DOWN
practices.body: Name the worry you keep setting down politely and picking straight back up. This week, throw it — the verb is forceful: ‘This is Yours. You care about me, and I am not carrying it back out of this room.’ Pride and worry share a root, and both are cured by getting low.

practices.title: REFUSE THE ISOLATION
practices.body: Isolation is the lion’s favorite ground, and Peter takes it away by reminding a scattered church that their brothers are under the same pressure. Tell one trusted believer this week the thing you have been carrying alone. Resistance is standing firm together, not fighting alone.

practices.title: BRING HIM THE TEAR
practices.body: Name the place you are most torn right now and bring it to the Spirit as a net to be mended rather than a failure to be hidden: ‘You said You would do this Yourself.’ He does not merely get you through the little while. He repairs the tear, establishes, strengthens, and settles.

title: Clothe Yourselves with Humility
subtitle: from dust to eternal glory
keyVerse: May the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.

Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly;

But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.
To him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
Through Silvanus, our faithful brother, as I consider him, I have written to you briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand.
She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you. So does Mark, my son.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE CHIEF SHEPHERD
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about finishing strong by your own effort. It is about getting low, throwing what you carry onto the God to whom you matter, and trusting the four verbs He has promised to perform Himself.
lifePulls: You will not restore yourself. He will. And Peter, who denied his Lord beside one fire and was mended beside another on a beach, is exactly the right man to tell you so.
prayer: Father, I humble myself under Your mighty hand. You will lift me in due time. I will stop trying to do it myself. I throw this worry onto You, because You care for me. Jesus, You knelt with a towel. Let me serve someone unseen today. Keep me watchful, and keep me beside my brothers. God of all grace, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle me. To You be the glory forever. Amen.

bottomLine: Tie on the servant’s apron, get low under the mighty hand of God, and throw every worry onto Him, because He cares for you. Stand firm against the adversary, and do not stand alone. The suffering is a little while; the God of all grace will Himself perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you, and the glory He called you to is eternal.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the climb. You have been trying to get up out of the low place the only way the world knows — by rising: by being seen, being right, being needed, securing the position. And the climbing has produced the very exhaustion it was meant to cure, because a soul that must hold itself up never gets to rest.

So hear the sentence that ends this letter’s long argument. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The way up is down. The lifting is His work, and He does it at the right hour, and you are not late. Get under the hand that is mighty enough to be worth trusting, and while you are down there, throw everything you have been carrying onto Him — not set down gently and retrieved, but flung. And hear why: because he cares for you. Not because worry is unproductive. Because you matter to Him.

And then tie on the apron. Peter chooses a word for a slave’s work-apron, and he chooses it because he cannot forget a certain night — his Master rising from supper, laying aside His garment, wrapping a towel around Himself, kneeling on the floor to wash the feet of men who would abandon Him before dawn. Peter objected. Thirty years later he writes to the churches and hands them that same picture. Not an abstraction. A memory.

So stand firm, and do not stand alone; your brothers across the world are in the same fire. And then rest in the four verbs that close the letter, and in the two words that stand in front of them: he himself will mend you, establish you, strengthen you, settle you. You will not restore yourself. He will — the God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in Christ Jesus. The suffering is a little while. The glory does not end. Lift your eyes off the dust you have been clinging to, off the climb, off the little while — and onto the eternal glory to which you were called. From dust, to a living hope, to glory. Rise.
closingVerse: May the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you. To him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
carry: Where have you been trying to lift yourself out of the dust — and what would it look like this week to get low under the mighty hand of God and let Him do it in due time?
